newsitem.title: UK: Denmark and Sweden to shun EMU for now.
newsitem.headline: Denmark and Sweden to shun EMU for now.

text.p: Denmark and Sweden appeared in good shape on Wednesday in a survey of their fitness for European economic and monetary union (EMU) but public scepticism is likely to keep them from joining at the start.
A Reuters poll of 32 economists across Europe showed Denmark and Sweden were expected to meet the inflation and long-term interest rate criteria for joining EMU.

They were both forecast to bring their budget deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 but in line with most countries, they were not expected to reduce their debt-to-GDP ratios to 60 percent.
Denmark is already in Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM), another precondition for EMU entry. Sweden has chosen to stay out.
But despite the rosy bill of health, analysts said both countries were likely to opt out because public opinion was against federalism.

"Danish and Swedish people are not willing to give up power to people who have not been elected democratically and cannot be controlled," said Gerhardt Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Germany.
In 1992 Denmark voted against EMU in a referendum.
After the government negotiated an opt-out from the single currency, the Maastricht Treaty was endorsed in a second referendum in 1993.
They also renegotiated their position on some defence clauses and on foreign policy integration.
According to recent opinion polls, Swedish people do not like the mechanisms of the European Union (EU). They want to stay on the sidelines and observe new developments, analysts say.
"Business leaders, bankers and the (central) Riksbank believe Sweden should join EMU but the Swedish government is split fairly evenly down the middle," said Grebe.
Sweden has a general election timetabled in 1998. Analysts expect the current government to clarify its position at the party conference this summer.
Sweden will also be watching this summer's inter- governmental conference of European Union (EU) leaders and finance ministers to gauge the extent of proposals for a federal Europe.
"It is a well-known fact that France and Germany want to create a political union to complement monetary union. People will be watching to see how far they go," one analyst said.
Despite the public and political scepticism, the Riksbank has no doubts about EMU entry.
The central bank said Sweden should join from the start, because delay could damage the Swedish economy.

"The economic benefits and the possibility of influencing the future direction of monetary policy leads the Riksbank governing board to conclude that Sweden should participate in EMU from the start," the central bank said.
While the Swedish people have adopted a wait-and-see attitude, some Danes have taken matters into their own hands.
A challenge to EMU has been lodged in a case at the country's constitutional court. A final decision may not come until the projected launch date for EMU at the start of 1999.
